pr_body:
Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/46075

PR enables trimming and AOT analysis on `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.Results` and fixes warnings.

* Adds trim warnings to methods that take `object routeValues`. Reflection is used to get property values.
* ~Adds safe overloads of warning methods that take `RouteValueDictionary`. This is the same pattern we used for `LinkGenerator` extension methods. Will need API review.~ Follow up task https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/46229
* ~Adds a reflection fallback for calling static `PopulateMetadata` method.~
* Adds temporary suppressions around `Response.WriteAsJsonAsync` and `ProblemDetails.Extensions` calls. I'm guessing the warnings will be removed from these with https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/45886
pr_comments: Seeing the changes to the results that generate links by using reflection on an object makes me think we should have generic overloads where we can mark them with DAM attributes.

That would solve trimming. However, without dynamic code generation, the properties would still be accessed using slow reflection in AOT. I don't think we should encourage that.

https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/4535ea1263e9a24ca8d37b7266797fe1563b8b12/src/Shared/PropertyHelper/PropertyHelper.cs#L214-L243

Reflection isn’t slow with AOT. Now that we’re doing the work I think it’s time to quantify this on NativeAOT.

cc @jkotas

> Reflection isn’t slow with AOT. Now that we’re doing the work I think it’s time to quantify this on NativeAOT.

I am not sure how fast it is today. 

We have work planned for ,NET 8 to make reflection fast (on all runtimes). https://github.com/dotnet/designs/pull/286 is the design document.

cc @steveharter

> * Adds temporary suppressions around `Response.WriteAsJsonAsync` and `ProblemDetails.Extensions` calls. I'm guessing the warnings will be removed from these with [Making `JsonOptions` AOT/Trimmer-safe with EnsureJsonTrimmability switch #45886](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/45886)

This PR should remove all Json related wanings https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/46008

> Reflection isn’t slow with AOT. Now that we’re doing the work I think it’s time to quantify this on NativeAOT.
> 
> cc @jkotas

I wrote some benchmarks:

```cs
public class JitBenchmarks
{
    [Benchmark]
    public RouteValueDictionary RawDictionary() => new RouteValueDictionary { ["foo"] = "One", ["bar"] = "Two", ["baz"] = "Three" };

    [Benchmark]
    public RouteValueDictionary PropertyReflection() => new RouteValueDictionary(new { foo = "One", bar = "Two", baz = "Three" });
}

[SimpleJob(RuntimeMoniker.NativeAot80)]
public class AotBenchmarks
{
    [Benchmark]
    public RouteValueDictionary RawDictionary() => new RouteValueDictionary { ["foo"] = "One", ["bar"] = "Two", ["baz"] = "Three" };

    [Benchmark]
    public RouteValueDictionary PropertyReflection() => new RouteValueDictionary(new { foo = "One", bar = "Two", baz = "Three" });
}

public class Program
{
    public static void Main(string[] args)
    {
        _ = BenchmarkRunner.Run(new[] { typeof (AotBenchmarks), typeof(JitBenchmarks) } );
    }
}
```

JIT:
```
BenchmarkDotNet=v0.13.4, OS=Windows 11 (10.0.22621.1105)
AMD Ryzen 7 5800X, 1 CPU, 16 logical and 8 physical cores
.NET SDK=8.0.100-alpha.1.23060.5
  [Host]     : .NET 8.0.0 (8.0.23.5802), X64 RyuJIT AVX2
  DefaultJob : .NET 8.0.0 (8.0.23.5802), X64 RyuJIT AVX2


|             Method |     Mean |    Error |   StdDev |
|------------------- |---------:|---------:|---------:|
|      RawDictionary | 18.09 ns | 0.337 ns | 0.581 ns |
| PropertyReflection | 28.57 ns | 0.381 ns | 0.318 ns |
```

AOT:
```
BenchmarkDotNet=v0.13.4, OS=Windows 11 (10.0.22621.1105)
AMD Ryzen 7 5800X, 1 CPU, 16 logical and 8 physical cores
.NET SDK=8.0.100-alpha.1.23060.5
  [Host]        : .NET 8.0.0 (8.0.23.5802), X64 RyuJIT AVX2
  NativeAOT 8.0 : .NET 8.0.0-alpha.1.23058.2, X64 NativeAOT AVX2

Job=NativeAOT 8.0  Runtime=NativeAOT 8.0

|             Method |     Mean |    Error |   StdDev |
|------------------- |---------:|---------:|---------:|
|      RawDictionary | 24.91 ns | 0.531 ns | 0.443 ns |
| PropertyReflection | 41.66 ns | 0.865 ns | 1.124 ns |
```

AOT seems generally slower, but native AOT reflection isn't that far off compiled expressions.

My other concern is the number of overloads. We have `Redirect(object values)` today. Choices to add:

* Add `Redirect(RouteValueDictionary values)`. This is consistent with what was added to link generation for trimming.
* Add `Redirect<[DynamicallyAccessedMembers(DynamicallyAccessedMemberTypes.PublicProperties)] TRouteValues>(TRouteValues values)`. Would also catch method calls with `RouteValueDictionary`. The downside is it would include all public properties from `RouteValueDictionary`, but that isn't important.
* Add both.

I thought about this more, and generics + `DynamicallyAccessedMembers` doesn't work with `Nullable<T>`.

If the value is `Nullable<T>`, then `DynamicallyAccessedMembers` on the method instructs `Nullable<T>` to preserve its properties, not the actual value of `T`.

> If the value is Nullable<T>, then DynamicallyAccessedMembers on the method instructs Nullable<T> to preserve its properties, not the actual value of T.

Sounds like something we can ask @vitek-karas about? Seems like it could be fixable no?

Ok! I didn't check this, I just guessed behavior. I'm sure I've seen linker warnings coming from doing `type = Nullable.GetUnderlyingType(type)`, and the new type loses all the annotated linker data. Was it my imagination? Or is this a recent change?

The special handling of `Nullable<T>` should solve the problem I mentioned.

The `All` annotation would make this work - at least in terms of what is removed. `All` keeps all members on the type, regardless of if they're public/private and it propagates to base class and all interfaces. Note that it also applies to all nested types - hopefully that will not cause size problems.

It might still produce warnings though because trimming analysis doesn't see through collections, so `GetInterfaces` returns unannotated values. So it would require a suppression unfortunately.

I think we can mark the existing methods as unsafe and discuss a way forward based on what you've discovered. 

@jaredpar this is a ref count for the API that lets us set an attribute to influence overload resolution for preferred methods.
All feedback applied. Please take a look.

> @jaredpar this is a ref count for the API that lets us set an attribute to influence overload resolution for preferred methods.

Is this another case where we want to effectively _remove_ an old overload and replace it with a new one? Basically the new one completely subsumes the older one?

> Is this another case where we want to effectively remove an old overload and replace it with a new one? Basically the new one completely subsumes the older one?

Yes. Specifically, it's coming up with this pattern:

```C#
void MethodThatTakesObject(object obj) { }
```

Oh, no we need to see if we can make trimmable, the attributes only work:

```C#
void MethodThatTakesObject<[Attribute]T>(T obj) { }
```

This feels kinda messy.

Note that the pattern of 

```C#
void MethodThatTakesObject(object obj) {   // do something with `obj.GetType()` }
```

=>

```C#
void MethodThatTakesObject<[DynamicallyAccessedMembers] T>(T obj) { }
```

Isn't necessarily a valid replacement because of inheritance. For example in the code

```C#
IDisposable d = new FileStream(...);
MethodThatTakesObject(d);
```

The `[DynamicallyAccessedMembers]` attribute would apply to `IDisposable` and not `FileStream`. Whereas in the `object` overload that calls `obj.GetType()`, the Type being inspected is `FileStream`.
Polymorphism breaks the trimmer, but that's not the point here (especially in this example).
All outstanding feedback applied. Please review 🙏

issue_context.title: [AOT] Annotate Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.Results for trimming and AOT
issue_context.body: `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.Results` is used by minimal API. It is currently unannotated. Because it is unannotated, minimal API apps that use results will get warnings from unresolved trimming and AOT issues in this assembly.

review_comments:
I missed this in @brunolins16's PR

The way we do this in dotnet/runtime is:

```C#
[ConditionalTheory(typeof(RemoteExecutor), nameof(RemoteExecutor.IsSupported))]
```

Do we need 2 separate attributes? Are we using the same `ConditionalTheory` attribute here as in dotnet/runtime?
We use separate attributes everywhere else in ASP.NET Core. IMO lets keep the current pattern.
Sounds good to me.
Can you link to https://github.com/dotnet/linker/issues/2715? This should be reverted when that is fixed.
Why are we marking these helpers as safe?
To make all the ResultsOfT safe.
What does that mean? Who is calling into it from safe code?
It won't call this from the source generator (see my other comment).
Why use the DAM attributes here at all? This is only called from other linker unfriendly code right?
These won't be called from the source generator is my point, I guess.

How would source generators get this metadata without calling `IEndpointMetadataProvider.PopulateMetadata`? All it will see is a return type that implements the interface. It doesn't know about these nested results. Unless there is a special case added for Results of T. But that seems unnecessary when this PR makes it AOT safe.

The source generators can just invoke the methods statically (that's what the prototype does already).

https://github.com/davidfowl/uController/blob/7c1e8f3db1c6a20738eff792386696ff89d4d7e7/GeneratedOutput/RouteBuilderExtensions.g.cs#L136-L137

This is what we're going to do. Also for Results<T0..TN>

Ok, so there will be a special case added in the generator for `Results<...>` then?

What is the actionable feedback here? Do you want me to revert the change to make `Results<...>` types unsafe? The change required to make it safe was just some DAM attributes. I'd prefer to leave it as it is.

If you do want it reverted, then I think suppressions will need to be added to the explicit implementations of `Results<...>.PopulateMetadata`. The static interface is explicitly implemented on these types. That means if someone does call it that there will be no feedback `PopulateMetadata` on these results is trimming/AOT unsafe.
Mark `ResultsOfTHelper` as `RequiresUnreferencedCode` and mark `Results<...>.PopulateMetadata` as `RequiresUnreferencedCode` and leave the implementation as is.

I placed `RequiresUnreferencedCode` and `RequiresGeneratedCode` on `Results<...>.PopulateMetadata` and get this error:

> Trim analysis error IL2046: Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.HttpResults.Results<TResult1,TResult2>.Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.Metadata.IEndpointMetadataProvider.PopulateMetadata(MethodInfo, EndpointBuilder): Member 'Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.HttpResults.Results<TResult1,TResult2>.Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.Metadata.IEndpointMetadataProvider.PopulateMetadata(MethodInfo, EndpointBuilder)' with 'RequiresUnreferencedCodeAttribute' implements interface member 'Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.Metadata.IEndpointMetadataProvider.PopulateMetadata(MethodInfo, EndpointBuilder)' without 'RequiresUnreferencedCodeAttribute'. 'RequiresUnreferencedCodeAttribute' annotations must match across all interface implementations or overrides.

This error prevents the scenario I mentioned above: an explicit implementation of an interface method with a warning is never seen, as it's always called through the interface.

There are two options:
* Suppressing the warnings in `Results<...>.PopulateMetadata`. If someone calls them with AOT or trimming then they could get runtime errors
* Keep the work already done to make it trim-safe. TBH I'm not sure why it should be reverted. I still would like to keep it as is.
I guess I don't understand the scenario where this needs to be trim safe. I might be missing something.
It's public API. We might not call it, but someone else who writes a web API framework that uses results could.

> There are two options:

> Suppressing the warnings in Results<...>.PopulateMetadata. If someone calls them with AOT or trimming then they could get runtime errors

That isn't really a viable option. We are striving to ensure that the app behaves the same with or without trimming/AOT, or you get a warning.
Why were we able to remove these suppressions? Can we do the same in Results.cs?

Can we write tests for this logic? I believe the new tests you wrote can be reused, you would just need to get the `System.Runtime.CompilerServices.RuntimeFeature.IsDynamicCodeSupported` feature switch set to `false`.

Here's an example of a test that flips a feature switch:

https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/3bacfee41700edf15fa3b4c607f5de434d9b8227/src/Http/Http.Extensions/test/JsonOptionsTests.cs#L15-L28

Done. This errors when using reflection. I've added an error message saying that a default interface implementation of PopulateMetadata isn't supported.

Realistically, no one is going to do it. And we will hopefully improve calling static interface methods in the future.
We should write tests for this.... As of now it is untested code, right?

Yes. Has the IsDynamicCodeSupported arrived in aspnetcore?

https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/45860

Yes, that one is in the current runtime we are using in aspnetcore. It's the DI switch that isn't here yet - blocked on a runtime bug in #46055.

Note even if the IsDynamicCodeSupported wasn't in, we could still write tests by making targeted console apps that are published for AOT and executed.
